speaking.title: Introduce Yourself
speaking.prompt: Say hello and introduce yourself. Say your name, your age and where you are from.
speaking.anchor: My name and age → Where I am from → What I like
speaking.collocations: my name is, I am from, nice to meet you, I like
speaking.phonetic: Say the "th" in "this" and "thanks" with your tongue between your teeth.

speaking.title: My Family
speaking.prompt: Talk about your family. Who is in your family? What are they like?
speaking.anchor: Who is in my family → Their names and ages → What I do with them
speaking.collocations: there are four people, my mother, my brother, we live together
speaking.phonetic: Say the final "s" in "parents" and "brothers" clearly.

speaking.title: My Daily Routine
speaking.prompt: Describe your day. What do you do in the morning, afternoon and evening?
speaking.anchor: Morning (get up, eat breakfast) → Afternoon (work or school) → Evening (dinner, sleep)
speaking.collocations: get up, have breakfast, go to work, go to bed
speaking.phonetic: Say the "s" at the end of "gets up" and "goes" when you talk about he or she.

speaking.title: My Home
speaking.prompt: Describe your home. Say what rooms it has and what you like in it.
speaking.anchor: Where my home is → The rooms in my home → My favourite room
speaking.collocations: I live in, there is a, living room, my favourite room
speaking.phonetic: Say "there is" and "there are" slowly and clearly, with a soft "th" sound.

speaking.title: My Favourite Food
speaking.prompt: Talk about your favourite food. Say what it is and when you eat it.
speaking.anchor: My favourite food → When and where I eat it → Why I like it
speaking.collocations: my favourite food is, I like to eat, it is delicious, for lunch
speaking.phonetic: Say the final "s" in "noodles" and "vegetables" as a "z" sound.

speaking.title: What I Can Do
speaking.prompt: Say what you can do and what you cannot do. Talk about three things.
speaking.anchor: Two things I can do → One thing I cannot do → What I want to learn
speaking.collocations: I can, I cannot, I can swim, I want to learn
speaking.phonetic: Say "can" short and soft, but say "can't" long and clear.

speaking.title: My Best Friend
speaking.prompt: Talk about your best friend. Say who he or she is and what you do together.
speaking.anchor: Who my friend is → What my friend looks like → What we do together
speaking.collocations: my best friend, he is tall, she has long hair, we play together
speaking.phonetic: Say the "h" in "he", "his" and "home" with a little air from your mouth.

speaking.title: My School or My Work
speaking.prompt: Talk about your school or your work. Say where it is and what you do there.
speaking.anchor: Where it is → What I do there → Who I meet there
speaking.collocations: I go to school, I work in, every day, at nine o'clock
speaking.phonetic: Say the "s" at the start of "school" and "student" with a short, clear sound.

speaking.title: My Weekend
speaking.prompt: Talk about your weekend. What do you do on Saturday and Sunday?
speaking.anchor: What I do on Saturday → What I do on Sunday → Who I am with
speaking.collocations: on Saturday, go shopping, watch TV, visit my family
speaking.phonetic: Say the final "s" in "weekends" and "Sundays" clearly.

speaking.title: My Town
speaking.prompt: Describe your town or city. Say what places are in it and what you like.
speaking.anchor: Where my town is → Places in my town → What I like about it
speaking.collocations: there is a park, near my house, a big city, I like it
speaking.phonetic: Say the "r" in "park" and "market" with your tongue back, not touching the roof of your mouth.

speaking.title: My Clothes and Colours
speaking.prompt: Say what clothes you wear today. Say the colours.
speaking.anchor: What I wear today → The colours → My favourite clothes
speaking.collocations: I am wearing, a blue shirt, black shoes, my favourite colour
speaking.phonetic: Say the final "s" in "clothes" and "shoes" as a "z" sound.

speaking.title: My Pet or My Favourite Animal
speaking.prompt: Talk about a pet or your favourite animal. Say what it looks like and what it does.
speaking.anchor: What animal it is → What it looks like → What it likes to do
speaking.collocations: I have a dog, it is small, it likes to eat, it is very cute
speaking.phonetic: Say the "d" at the end of "good" and "friend" with a quick touch of your tongue.

speaking.title: A Trip You Took
speaking.prompt: Talk about a trip you took. Where did you go, and what did you do?
speaking.anchor: Where and when you went → What you did there → Why you liked it
speaking.collocations: go on a trip, stay in a hotel, take photos, have a great time
speaking.phonetic: Past -ed endings: say 'visited' as 'VIZ-i-tid', but 'walked' as 'walkt' (one sound).

speaking.title: My Best Friend
speaking.prompt: Talk about your best friend. What is he or she like?
speaking.anchor: Who the person is → What he or she looks like and is like → What you do together
speaking.collocations: have known someone for years, be good at, spend time with, get on well with
speaking.phonetic: Word stress: put the stress on the first part of 'FRIENDly' and 'FUNny'.

speaking.title: Last Weekend
speaking.prompt: Tell me about what you did last weekend.
speaking.anchor: What you did on Saturday → What you did on Sunday → How you felt about it
speaking.collocations: stay at home, meet friends, go shopping, watch a film
speaking.phonetic: Past -ed endings: 'played' ends with a 'd' sound, 'cooked' ends with a 't' sound.

speaking.title: A Shop You Like
speaking.prompt: Talk about a shop you like. What do you buy there?
speaking.anchor: Where the shop is → What you buy there → Why you like it
speaking.collocations: be open until, a good price, try on clothes, pay by card
speaking.phonetic: Weak forms: say 'a cup of tea' as 'a CUP uv TEA'; 'of' is short and quiet.

speaking.title: Plans for Next Week
speaking.prompt: What are you going to do next week? Talk about your plans.
speaking.anchor: Your plan for work or study → Your plan for the evenings → Your plan for the weekend
speaking.collocations: be going to, next week, have a meeting, visit my family
speaking.phonetic: Weak forms: 'going to' sounds like 'gonna' in fast speech, and 'to' is short.

speaking.title: Advice for a Visitor
speaking.prompt: A friend wants to visit your town. Give some advice.
speaking.anchor: The best time to come → Places to see and food to try → Things to be careful about
speaking.collocations: you should, the best time to visit, try the local food, take an umbrella
speaking.phonetic: Word stress: say 'ADvice' with stress on the first part, and 'viSIT' on the second.

speaking.title: My Daily Routine
speaking.prompt: Describe a normal day in your life.
speaking.anchor: Morning routine → Work or study during the day → Evening and bedtime
speaking.collocations: get up early, have breakfast, go to work, go to bed
speaking.phonetic: Sentence stress: say the important words louder, like 'I GET UP at SIX'.

speaking.title: My Home
speaking.prompt: Describe your home. Which room do you like best?
speaking.anchor: Where you live and who lives with you → The rooms in your home → Your favourite room and why
speaking.collocations: live in a flat, share a room, next to, a big window
speaking.phonetic: Word stress: say 'BEDroom' and 'LIVing room' with stress on the first part.

speaking.title: My Favourite Food
speaking.prompt: Talk about your favourite food. How do you make it, or where do you eat it?
speaking.anchor: What the food is → What is in it or where you eat it → Why you love it
speaking.collocations: taste good, cook a meal, a lot of, too spicy
speaking.phonetic: Weak forms: say 'a lot of rice' as 'a LOT uv RICE'; the word 'of' is quiet.

speaking.title: My Hobby
speaking.prompt: Talk about a hobby you enjoy. When and where do you do it?
speaking.anchor: What the hobby is → When and where you do it → Why you enjoy it
speaking.collocations: in my free time, be interested in, once a week, learn how to
speaking.phonetic: Word stress: say 'HOBby' and 'FAvourite' with stress on the first part.

speaking.title: A Time You Were Ill
speaking.prompt: Talk about a time you were ill. What happened?
speaking.anchor: What was wrong → What you did to feel better → How long it took
speaking.collocations: have a headache, see a doctor, take some medicine, feel better
speaking.phonetic: Past -ed endings: say 'needed' as 'NEE-did', but 'stayed' as 'stayd' (one sound).

speaking.title: Weather and Seasons
speaking.prompt: Talk about the weather in your country. What is your favourite season?
speaking.anchor: The weather in each season → Your favourite season → What you do in that season
speaking.collocations: be hot and sunny, rain a lot, in the summer, wear a coat
speaking.phonetic: Word stress: say 'WEAther' and 'SEAson' with stress on the first part.

speaking.title: A Memorable Experience
speaking.prompt: Talk about a memorable experience you have had. Say what happened, who was with you and why you still remember it.
speaking.anchor: Set the scene (when and where) → Tell what happened → Say why it is special to you
speaking.collocations: unforgettable experience, take place, to be honest, looking back
speaking.phonetic: Stress the key words in each sentence, for example 'It was the BEST day of my LIFE', and say small words like 'the' and 'of' quickly.

speaking.title: A Problem and How You Solved It
speaking.prompt: Describe a problem you had and explain how you solved it. What did you learn from it?
speaking.anchor: Explain the problem → Describe what you did to fix it → Say what you learned
speaking.collocations: deal with a problem, come up with a solution, ask for help, in the end
speaking.phonetic: Link words that join consonant to vowel, for example 'ask_for_help' sounds like 'as-kfor-help'.

speaking.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Social Media
speaking.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of social media? Give your own opinion.
speaking.anchor: Main advantages (stay in touch, share news) → Main disadvantages (waste of time, privacy) → Your opinion and reason
speaking.collocations: keep in touch with, waste of time, on the other hand, in my opinion
speaking.phonetic: Use rising intonation on each item in a list and falling intonation on the last one: 'friends, news, photos and videos'.

speaking.title: Your Plans for the Future
speaking.prompt: Talk about your plans for the next five years. What do you hope to do, and what might stop you?
speaking.anchor: Your main plan (study, work or travel) → Steps you will take → Possible problems and how you will deal with them
speaking.collocations: be planning to, make progress, achieve a goal, if everything goes well
speaking.phonetic: Stress the important verb in plans, for example 'I'm going to STUDY abroad', and say 'going to' quickly as 'gonna' in relaxed speech.

speaking.title: A Book or Film You Recommend
speaking.prompt: Recommend a book or a film to a friend. Say what it is about and why you think they will enjoy it.
speaking.anchor: Name it and say what it is about → What you liked most → Who you recommend it to and why
speaking.collocations: be based on, the main character, well worth watching, I would recommend
speaking.phonetic: Make your voice go up and louder on the words that show feeling, for example 'It was REALLY exciting'.

speaking.title: Life in a Big City or a Small Town
speaking.prompt: Would you prefer to live in a big city or a small town? Give reasons for your answer.
speaking.anchor: Say which you prefer → Give two reasons with examples → Mention one good point about the other place
speaking.collocations: public transport, cost of living, peace and quiet, there are plenty of
speaking.phonetic: Stress the contrast words in a comparison, for example 'The city is NOISY but the town is QUIET'.

speaking.title: A Person Who Has Helped You
speaking.prompt: Talk about a person who has helped you in your life. Say who the person is, how they helped you and how you feel about them.
speaking.anchor: Who the person is → How they helped you → What you would like to say to them now
speaking.collocations: look up to, be grateful for, support someone, get on well with
speaking.phonetic: Say the 'ed' endings clearly, for example 'helped' ends with a /t/ sound and 'supported' ends with /id/.

speaking.title: Should Students Wear a School Uniform?
speaking.prompt: Do you think students should wear a school uniform? Explain your opinion with reasons.
speaking.anchor: Your opinion → Two reasons with examples → What people who disagree might say and your answer
speaking.collocations: feel equal, express yourself, I strongly believe that, on the whole
speaking.phonetic: Pause briefly after your opinion, then give your reasons: 'I think so, because...'.

speaking.title: A Trip You Have Taken
speaking.prompt: Describe a trip you have taken. Where did you go, what did you do and would you go there again?
speaking.anchor: Where you went and who with → The best and worst parts → Whether you would go again
speaking.collocations: go sightseeing, book a hotel, local food, have a great time
speaking.phonetic: Use past tense endings clearly in a story, for example 'visited', 'stayed', 'enjoyed'.

speaking.title: Working from Home or in an Office
speaking.prompt: Is it better to work from home or in an office? Say what you think and why.
speaking.anchor: Benefits of working from home → Benefits of working in an office → Your choice and reason
speaking.collocations: save time, work as a team, stay focused, it depends on
speaking.phonetic: Stress 'but' and the word after it to show a change of idea: 'It is flexible, but it can be LONELY'.

speaking.title: Healthy Habits in Daily Life
speaking.prompt: What do you do to stay healthy? Talk about your habits and say what you could do better.
speaking.anchor: Your good habits (food, sport, sleep) → One habit you want to change → Advice for a friend
speaking.collocations: get enough sleep, take exercise, eat a balanced diet, give up
speaking.phonetic: Link 'a' and 'of' to the next word, for example 'a lot of' sounds like 'a-lo-tuv'.

speaking.title: Learning English: Your Experience
speaking.prompt: Talk about how you have been learning English. What helps you most and what is difficult for you?
speaking.anchor: Why and how you started → What helps you most → Your goal for the future
speaking.collocations: make mistakes, improve my speaking, practise every day, keep going
speaking.phonetic: Say long words with the stress in the right place, for example 'imPROVE' and 'PRACtise'.

speaking.title: The Automation Paradox in Knowledge Work
speaking.prompt: As artificial intelligence automates cognitive and analytical tasks, assess whether human expertise will be amplified or degraded over the next decade.
speaking.anchor: Past baseline (manual analysis) → Present disruption (generative tools) → Future equilibrium (human-in-the-loop critical judgment)
speaking.collocations: disruptive technology, cognitive bandwidth, human-in-the-loop, single point of failure
speaking.phonetic: Nuclear stress on contrastive verbs: 'AMPLIFIED versus DEGRADED'; crisp catenation across 'human-in-the-loop'.

speaking.title: Remote Work and Corporate Velocity
speaking.prompt: Does asynchronous distributed work inherently diminish organizational agility and creative serendipity, or does it maximize deep productivity?
speaking.anchor: Thesis (agility vs. deep focus) → Structural trade-off (communication friction) → Strategic resolution (hybrid cadence)
speaking.collocations: organizational velocity, deep work, asynchronous communication, trade-off
speaking.phonetic: Downward terminal intonation on declarative claims; avoid upward question inflections on non-questions.

speaking.title: Algorithmic Echo Chambers and Societal Polarization
speaking.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which recommender systems and algorithmic curation are fracturing social consensus and civic discourse.
speaking.anchor: Root cause (engagement-driven algorithms) → Psychological mechanism (confirmation bias) → Societal fallout & systemic remediation
speaking.collocations: algorithmic bias, confirmation bias, civic discourse, polarization
speaking.phonetic: Smooth linking across 'fracturing social consensus'; rhythmic pulsing on polysyllabic nominalizations.

speaking.title: The Ethics of Gene Editing (CRISPR)
speaking.prompt: Should genetic engineering in humans be restricted exclusively to therapeutic cures, or is human enhancement an inevitable technological progression?
speaking.anchor: Dichotomy (therapeutic necessity vs. enhancement hubris) → Slippery slope argument → Regulatory governance framework
speaking.collocations: genetic modification, ethical boundary, slippery slope, regulatory framework
speaking.phonetic: Deliberate pause before the pivot word 'However'; clear articulation of the /str/ cluster in 'restricted'.

speaking.title: The Viability of Universal Basic Income (UBI)
speaking.prompt: Analyze whether Universal Basic Income provides a necessary safety net against technological unemployment or creates macroeconomic disincentives to labor.
speaking.anchor: Economic justification (safety net against displacement) → Counter-argument (fiscal inflation & labor disincentive) → Balanced synthesis
speaking.collocations: economic safety net, fiscal sustainability, labor participation, inflationary pressure
speaking.phonetic: Primary stress on the final noun of the compound 'Universal Basic INcome'; maintain steady breath support across long compound sentences.

speaking.title: Monopoly Power of Big Tech Platforms
speaking.prompt: Argue whether global tech conglomerates constitute natural utilities that require aggressive antitrust breakup or dynamic drivers of capital reinvestment.
speaking.anchor: Market dominance reality → Anti-competitive harm (stifled innovation) → Regulatory dilemma (utility status vs. market dynamism)
speaking.collocations: antitrust scrutiny, monopolistic practices, barrier to entry, capital expenditure
speaking.phonetic: Contrastive stress: 'regulators seek to DISMANTLE, while executives seek to DEFEND'.

speaking.title: Standardized Testing versus Holistic Evaluation
speaking.prompt: Critique the role of standardized academic testing in higher education admissions in light of equity, predictive validity, and student potential.
speaking.anchor: Original objective (objective benchmark) → Inherent systemic bias (socioeconomic disparity) → Modern alternative (portfolio & diagnostic evaluation)
speaking.collocations: standardized testing, predictive validity, socioeconomic disparity, holistic assessment
speaking.phonetic: Catenation in 'standardized-testing-in-higher-education'; suppress vocal filler ('um', 'like') during transitions.

speaking.title: The Commercialization of Space Exploration
speaking.prompt: Assess whether private commercial aerospace enterprises are accelerating humanity's cosmic expansion or creating an ungoverned domain of corporate exploitation.
speaking.anchor: State-led stagnation → Private agility and capital infusion → Geopolitical and legal vacuums needing treaty frameworks
speaking.collocations: space exploration, private enterprise, capital infusion, legal vacuum
speaking.phonetic: Upward pitch reset at the onset of major structural transitions ('First and foremost', 'Crucially').

speaking.title: Cashless Economies and Financial Surveillance
speaking.prompt: Discuss the societal trade-offs between the transactional efficiency of digital payments and the systematic erosion of financial privacy.
speaking.anchor: Operational convenience → State and corporate surveillance risks → Vulnerability of marginalized demographics without digital literacy
speaking.collocations: transactional efficiency, financial surveillance, central bank digital currency, digital divide
speaking.phonetic: Stress the first syllable of 'CASHless' and the second of 'fiNANcial'; release the final /s/ cleanly.

speaking.title: Urban Density versus Suburban Sprawl
speaking.prompt: Defend high-density, transit-oriented urbanism against the suburban ideal from environmental, economic, and mental well-being perspectives.
speaking.anchor: Ecological imperative (carbon footprint) → Municipal economics (infrastructure cost) → Human connectivity vs. isolation
speaking.collocations: transit-oriented development, carbon footprint, suburban sprawl, municipal infrastructure
speaking.phonetic: Pacing variation: accelerate through supporting examples, decelerate on core takeaway axioms.

speaking.title: Degrowth versus Green Growth Economics
speaking.prompt: Can continuous GDP growth be decoupled from environmental degradation through clean technology, or must developed nations embrace economic degrowth?
speaking.anchor: Ecological limits of growth → The technological decoupling fallacy → The socioeconomic realignment required for steady-state economics
speaking.collocations: decoupling economic growth, ecological balance, renewable energy transition, circular economy
speaking.phonetic: Nuclear stress on opposing economic paradigms: 'GREEN GROWTH versus RADICAL DEGROWTH'.

speaking.title: Surveillance Capitalism and Predictive Behavioral Modeling
speaking.prompt: How does the commercial extraction of behavioral surplus reshape individual human autonomy and democratic decision-making?
speaking.anchor: Data extraction mechanism → Predictive behavioral modification → Subversion of consumer and voter sovereignty
speaking.collocations: behavioral surplus, predictive analytics, data harvesting, democratic integrity
speaking.phonetic: Rhythmic cadence on the rule of three: 'monitored, modeled, and manipulated'.

speaking.title: The Crisis of Reproducibility in Modern Science
speaking.prompt: Investigate why a substantial fraction of published peer-reviewed studies fail replication and propose concrete institutional remedies.
speaking.anchor: Perverse academic incentives ('publish or perish') → Statistical malpractices (p-hacking, publication bias) → Structural reform (open data, pre-registration)

speaking.phonetic: Crisp schwa reductions in unstressed syllables: 'reproducibility', 'methodology', 'experiment'.

speaking.title: Censorship versus Content Moderation on Public Squares
speaking.prompt: Where should the boundary lie between protecting freedom of expression and curbing malicious disinformation on digital platforms?
speaking.anchor: Free speech absolutism vs. harm prevention → The gatekeeping dilemma of private tech platforms → Transparent democratic oversight
speaking.collocations: freedom of expression, public interest, content moderation, malicious disinformation
speaking.phonetic: Clear articulation of final consonant stops: /d/ in 'protecting freedom of speech and public trust'.

speaking.title: The Longevity Economy and Demographics
speaking.prompt: How will unprecedented population aging in developed societies reshape pension solvency, healthcare delivery, and generational wealth distribution?
speaking.anchor: Demographic inversion (shrinking workforce) → Fiscal strain on healthcare & pensions → Innovations in automated eldercare and retirement age reforms
speaking.collocations: ageing population, pension solvency, healthcare infrastructure, generational equity
speaking.phonetic: Maintain energetic pitch variety across statistical explanations to avoid monotone pacing.

speaking.title: Neurotechnology and Cognitive Liberty
speaking.prompt: As brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) advance from medical restoration to consumer applications, what legal frameworks must be erected to protect neural privacy?
speaking.anchor: Technological horizon (medical to consumer BCIs) → The threat of neural surveillance → Legal codification of cognitive liberty
speaking.collocations: brain-computer interface, cognitive liberty, neural privacy, cutting-edge technology
speaking.phonetic: Contrastive emphasis: 'protect not merely PHYSICAL actions, but INNER THOUGHTS'.

speaking.title: The Value of a Humanities Degree in a STEM-Centric Era
speaking.prompt: In an employment market dominated by technical and engineering skills, defend the intrinsic and pragmatic utility of philosophy, literature, and history.
speaking.anchor: Perceived economic obsolescence → Foundational competencies (critical hermeneutics, ethical reasoning, rhetorical synthesis) → The human moat against automation
speaking.collocations: critical thinking, ethical reasoning, qualitative analysis, holistic education

speaking.collocations: decentralized finance, systemic risk, smart contract, regulatory arbitrage

speaking.collocations: environmental impact, carbon footprint, consumerist culture, regulatory mandate

speaking.title: Urban Congestion Pricing Schemes

speaking.phonetic: Slow the tempo and lower the pitch range on the key sentence; keep it in a single tone unit with a clear final fall so the message is not softened into ambiguity, then leave a full pause.

speaking.title: The Turning Point: Narrating a Personal Story
speaking.prompt: Recount a moment that changed the direction of your life or career, making clear what you believed before, what happened, and how you see it now.
speaking.anchor: Backstory (past perfect and 'used to': who I had been) → The pivotal moment (past simple and past continuous: what happened) → Reflection (present perfect and present simple: what has changed since)
speaking.collocations: little did I know, in hindsight, a defining moment, it finally clicked, it dawned on me
speaking.phonetic: Mark the climax with a pause before the key clause and a high-onset fall on the pivotal word; use weak forms /həd/ and /wəz/ in the backstory so that stressed content words carry the rhythm.

speaking.title: Persuading an Unconvinced Audience
speaking.prompt: You are presenting a four-day working week pilot to a room of department heads who are openly doubtful. Win them over in two minutes.
speaking.anchor: Concede their concern (name the strongest objection first) → Reframe with a low-risk test (a time-limited pilot with clear success measures) → Call to action (the specific decision you want today)
speaking.collocations: I'm well aware that, the burden of proof, a low-risk trial, by the same token, what have we got to lose
speaking.phonetic: Use contrastive stress to pivot from their view to yours ('YOU see a cost; I see an INVESTMENT'); end the call to action on a decisive fall, not a rising tone that invites refusal.

speaking.title: Explaining a Complex Idea to a Twelve-Year-Old
speaking.prompt: Explain to a curious twelve-year-old how vaccines train the immune system, without jargon and without talking down to them.
speaking.anchor: Relatable analogy (a wanted poster for germs) → Mechanism in plain steps (practice run, memory, faster response) → Check understanding (invite a question and restate the idea in one line)
speaking.collocations: think of it like, in other words, the gist of it, it boils down to, does that make sense
speaking.phonetic: Keep tone units short with one nucleus each; use a rising tone on check questions ('Does that make SENSE? ↗'); place stress on the analogy keyword rather than on technical terms.

speaking.title: Negotiating a Compromise Between Two Teams
speaking.prompt: Two departments both claim the same limited budget for the coming year. As the mediator, propose a compromise that both sides can accept.
speaking.anchor: Map interests (what each team actually needs, not what it demands) → Explore trade-offs (sequencing, shared resources, conditions) → Package deal (restate the agreement and confirm commitment from both sides)
speaking.collocations: common ground, a sticking point, split the difference, a win-win outcome, on condition that
speaking.phonetic: Fall-rise on conditional offers ('IF we can agree on timing ↘↗...'); keep a level, unhurried pitch to project neutrality; stress the contrasting possessives ('YOUR team... OUR side').

speaking.title: Raising a Glass: A Retirement Toast
speaking.prompt: Give a toast at the retirement dinner of a mentor who shaped your early career, balancing warmth, light-hearted wit and sincerity.
speaking.anchor: Hook anecdote (a vivid first memory of them) → Tribute (their qualities and their impact on others) → Toast (a forward-looking wish and the invitation to raise glasses)
speaking.collocations: it gives me great pleasure, leave a lasting legacy, go above and beyond, words cannot do justice, please join me in raising a glass
speaking.phonetic: Pause just before punchlines and before the final toast; use the weak form /tə/ in 'Here's to Sam' so that the name carries the nuclear stress on a warm, wide fall.

speaking.title: Handling a Hostile Question at a Press Conference
speaking.prompt: After you announce a product recall, a journalist accuses your company of covering up the defect for months. Respond calmly and honestly without becoming defensive.
speaking.anchor: Acknowledge and bridge (validate the concern without repeating the accusation) → Address the substance (what was known, when, and what was done) → Pivot to commitment (concrete corrective steps and accountability)
speaking.collocations: I understand why you would ask, let me be absolutely clear, with the benefit of hindsight, take full responsibility, the facts are as follows
speaking.phonetic: Keep the pitch range narrow and the tempo steady; avoid rising intonation on factual statements, which sounds uncertain; place nuclear stress on verbs of commitment ('we WILL publish the findings').

speaking.title: Hedging an Uncertain Forecast
speaking.prompt: Your director asks whether next year's sales will recover, but the data are mixed. Give a balanced forecast that is honest about uncertainty yet still useful for planning.
speaking.anchor: Best estimate (with an explicit level of confidence) → Key assumptions and risks (what could push the figure up or down) → Planning recommendation (scenarios and trigger points for review)
speaking.collocations: in all likelihood, barring any major shocks, err on the side of caution, by and large, a fair degree of uncertainty
speaking.phonetic: Fall-rise on hedges ('PROBably ↘↗') to signal reservation; stress modals of probability ('it MAY recover'); replace fillers with short silent pauses between tone units.

speaking.title: Critiquing a Work You Admire but Question
speaking.prompt: Describe a film, painting or novel you consider significant but flawed, assessing both its artistic achievement and its shortcomings.
speaking.anchor: Context and premise (what the work sets out to do) → Achievement (craft, imagery, performance) → Reservations and verdict (where it falls short and why it still matters)
speaking.collocations: strike a chord, a tour de force, fall flat, verge on the sentimental, stand the test of time
speaking.phonetic: Contrastive stress on evaluative pairs ('visually STUNNING but dramatically THIN'); fall-rise on the concessive 'admittedly'; slow the tempo for the final verdict.

writing.title: The Epistemic Hazards of Synthetic Information

meal.m: The ubiquitous proliferation of generative synthetic media fundamentally corrodes the epistemic integrity of modern jurisprudence by rendering authentic audio-visual evidence indistinguishable from fabricated artifacts.
meal.e: In federal courts, defense counsel have increasingly leveraged the 'liar's dividend'—a defense strategy whereby culpable defendants escape liability by alleging genuine surveillance footage is an AI deepfake.
meal.a: Because digital forensic toolkits invariably lag behind diffusion-model capabilities, evidentiary gatekeepers can no longer rely on traditional perceptual heuristics, forcing juries to operate in an epistemic vacuum where verifiable reality is conflated with algorithmic illusion.
meal.l: Consequently, unless strict cryptographic provenance standards are institutionalized at the hardware layer, the judicial system risks descending into a state of structural paralysis where no recording commands legal legitimacy.

writing.title: Algorithmic Pricing and Consumer Surplus

meal.m: Automated first-degree price discrimination enables dominant digital marketplaces to systematically expropriate consumer surplus and convert it into pure producer surplus through granular behavioral surveillance.
meal.e: Empirical pricing audits across major airline and hospitality aggregators demonstrate price discrepancies exceeding 35% for identical bookings based solely on user browsing history, device telemetry, and zip-code demographic profiling.
meal.a: By processing these high-dimensional data streams through predictive willingness-to-pay algorithms, platforms eradicate the traditional single-price market equilibrium, extracting the maximum financial reservation threshold from each transacting individual.
meal.l: This algorithmic rent extraction undermines market efficiency, effectively replacing transparent competition with opaque, asymmetric price exploitation.

writing.title: The Meritocracy Trap in Modern Higher Education

writing.title: A Formal Complaint about Unresolved Heating Failures

meal.m: Despite three written assurances since November, the heating system in our building remains unreliable, and I must now ask you to treat this matter as a formal complaint.
meal.e: On each occasion, an engineer attended, replaced a single component and left within the hour; on each occasion, the system failed again within days, leaving elderly residents on the upper floors without heating during the coldest weeks of the year.
meal.a: This pattern suggests that the underlying fault has never been diagnosed, only its symptoms addressed, and that your service agreement is being observed in letter rather than in spirit.
meal.l: I therefore request a full inspection by an independent engineer within fourteen days, together with written confirmation of the remedial work proposed, failing which I shall refer the matter to the relevant ombudsman.

writing.question: Write the central paragraph of a formal letter to a building management company complaining that repeated heating failures have not been resolved despite earlier assurances.
writing.masterSentence: Despite three written assurances since November, the heating system in our building remains unreliable, and I must now ask you to treat this matter as a formal complaint.
writing.stylistic: Measured formality without hostility, deliberate parallel repetition ('on each occasion'), the formal conditional 'failing which', precise deadlines and requests.

writing.title: Recommending a Trial Scheme in an Internal Report

meal.m: On balance, it is recommended that flexible start times be introduced on a six-month trial basis, subject to agreed core hours and a formal review at the end of the period.
meal.e: Feedback gathered from team leaders during the consultation indicated that the main obstacles to punctuality were childcare drop-offs and unreliable commuter services rather than any lack of commitment among staff.
meal.a: Allowing staff to begin at any point between 7.30 and 10.00, while requiring attendance during core hours, would address these practical constraints without compromising collaboration or client coverage.
meal.l: Should the review show no loss of productivity, the scheme could be made permanent; should problems emerge, the trial structure allows it to be withdrawn without contractual complications.

writing.question: Write the recommendation paragraph of an internal report advising senior management on whether to introduce flexible start times for office staff.
writing.masterSentence: On balance, it is recommended that flexible start times be introduced on a six-month trial basis, subject to agreed core hours and a formal review at the end of the period.
writing.stylistic: Impersonal passive ('it is recommended that'), mandative subjunctive ('be introduced'), paired inverted conditionals ('Should the review...; should problems...'), balanced alternatives.

writing.title: Reviewing an Ambitious Debut Novel

meal.m: For all its dazzling sentences, the novel never quite decides what story it wants to tell, and its brilliance arrives in flashes rather than as a sustained illumination.
meal.e: The opening chapters, set in a fading seaside town, are rendered with such sensory precision that the reader can almost taste the salt; yet the second half abandons this world for a hurried conspiracy plot that feels borrowed from another book.
meal.a: The problem is not a lack of talent but a surplus of ambition: the author seems reluctant to sacrifice any idea, and the narrative sags under the weight of competing intentions.
meal.l: Still, few debuts announce a voice this distinctive, and readers willing to forgive its excesses will find a writer worth following.

writing.question: Write the evaluative paragraph of a review of a debut novel that is stylistically ambitious but structurally uneven.
writing.masterSentence: For all its dazzling sentences, the novel never quite decides what story it wants to tell, and its brilliance arrives in flashes rather than as a sustained illumination.
writing.stylistic: Concessive opener ('For all its...'), sustained light-and-flash imagery, antithesis ('not a lack of talent but a surplus of ambition'), a balanced closing verdict.

writing.title: A Tribute to a Community Doctor

meal.m: For forty years, Ellen Marsh served this town as its family doctor in the conviction that listening was the most powerful instrument she carried.
meal.e: Patients recall consultations that ran well beyond their allotted time, house calls made through snowdrifts, and her habit of remembering the names of children she had delivered long after they had children of their own.
meal.a: Such devotion was not sentimental but clinical: she understood that an accurate diagnosis often depends on a patient feeling unhurried enough to mention the symptom they consider too trivial to raise.
meal.l: She leaves behind a generation who were not merely treated but known, and a standard of care against which her successors will measure themselves for years to come.

writing.question: Write a paragraph for a local newspaper paying tribute to a recently deceased family doctor who served the same community for four decades.
writing.masterSentence: For forty years, Ellen Marsh served this town as its family doctor in the conviction that listening was the most powerful instrument she carried.
writing.stylistic: Elegiac yet restrained tone, a concrete tricolon of memories, the 'not merely... but' contrast, a forward-looking close with a fronted preposition ('against which').

writing.title: Making the Case in a Cover Letter

meal.m: Over the past five years, I have learned that successful projects depend less on rigid plans than on the ability to keep diverse teams aligned when circumstances change.
meal.e: In my current role, I took over a delayed system migration involving three external vendors, introduced a weekly cross-team review, and renegotiated the delivery schedule so that the most critical services moved first.
meal.a: The experience taught me that transparency about setbacks builds more trust than optimistic reporting, and that stakeholders are far more forgiving of bad news delivered early than of surprises delivered late.
meal.l: I would welcome the opportunity to bring this approach to your team, particularly as you expand your portfolio of cross-border projects.

writing.question: Write the central paragraph of a cover letter for a project manager position, demonstrating relevant achievement without sounding boastful.
writing.masterSentence: Over the past five years, I have learned that successful projects depend less on rigid plans than on the ability to keep diverse teams aligned when circumstances change.
writing.stylistic: Modest first-person framing ('I have learned'), concrete action verbs in a tricolon, comparative balance ('less on... than on', 'delivered early... delivered late'), a courteous forward-looking close.

writing.title: Executive Summary of a Customer Retention Review

meal.m: This review finds that customer losses stem primarily from a poor onboarding experience rather than from pricing, and it proposes three targeted measures to reverse the trend within two quarters.
meal.e: Exit interviews and support records repeatedly describe new users struggling to configure the service in their first two weeks, while departing customers seldom cite cost as their main reason for leaving.
meal.a: The implication is that discounting, the remedy most often proposed internally, would reduce revenue without addressing the actual cause of dissatisfaction.
meal.l: The board is therefore asked to approve investment in guided onboarding, proactive check-ins during the first month and a simplified setup process, as detailed in Sections 3 to 5.

writing.question: Write the opening paragraph of an executive summary for a board reviewing why a subscription service is losing long-term customers.
writing.masterSentence: This review finds that customer losses stem primarily from a poor onboarding experience rather than from pricing, and it proposes three targeted measures to reverse the trend within two quarters.
writing.stylistic: Front-loaded findings, impersonal reporting verbs ('finds', 'proposes'), contrastive 'rather than', an explicit request for a decision with cross-references.

writing.title: An Op-Ed Opening in Support of Public Libraries

meal.m: Walk into any public library on a weekday morning and you will find the clearest rebuttal to the claim that libraries have outlived their purpose.
meal.e: A retired engineer is learning to video-call his grandchildren; a teenager without internet access at home is finishing her coursework; a newly arrived family is completing residency forms with the help of a librarian who speaks their language.
meal.a: None of these people has come for books alone; they have come for the one public space that asks nothing of them but quiet, and that offers in return access, expertise and dignity.
meal.l: To cut library budgets on the assumption that the internet has made them redundant is to mistake the building for the service, and to abandon precisely those citizens the internet has left behind.

writing.question: Write the opening paragraph of a newspaper opinion piece arguing that public libraries deserve renewed funding.
writing.masterSentence: Walk into any public library on a weekday morning and you will find the clearest rebuttal to the claim that libraries have outlived their purpose.
writing.stylistic: Imperative-conditional hook ('Walk into... and you will find'), a cinematic tricolon of vignettes separated by semicolons, singular agreement after 'None of these people has', an infinitival subject in the closing antithesis.

writing.title: Reflecting on a Failure that Taught More than Success

meal.m: It took the collapse of my first business to teach me that confidence and competence are not the same thing, however often they are mistaken for each other.
meal.e: I had launched the venture with a polished pitch and a loyal circle of supporters, yet within eighteen months I was closing its doors, having ignored every warning about cash flow because the warnings did not fit the story I was telling myself.
meal.a: Looking back, the failure was less a matter of bad luck than of selective attention: I listened to the voices that confirmed my plans and quietly dismissed the ones that questioned them.
meal.l: I still take risks, but I now seek out the most doubtful person in the room before committing, because I have learned that the objection I least want to hear is usually the one I most need to answer.

writing.question: Write a paragraph for a reflective personal essay about a failure that ultimately proved more instructive than any success.
writing.masterSentence: It took the collapse of my first business to teach me that confidence and competence are not the same thing, however often they are mistaken for each other.
writing.stylistic: Cleft-style opening ('It took... to teach me'), candid first-person retrospection, a perfect participle clause ('having ignored'), a chiastic close ('least want... most need').

writing.title: Proposing a Community Garden

meal.m: We propose to transform the disused lot on Mill Street into a community garden that would provide fresh produce, outdoor learning space and a shared meeting point for residents of all ages.
meal.e: Our residents' association has already secured volunteer commitments from local families, a nearby primary school has expressed interest in weekly gardening lessons, and a hardware supplier has offered tools at cost.
meal.a: Because the plot currently attracts illegal dumping and must be cleared periodically at public expense, the project would convert a recurring liability into a maintained asset at minimal cost to the council.
meal.l: We therefore request a three-year lease of the site at a nominal rent, with a progress report submitted to the council at the end of each growing season.

writing.question: Write the core paragraph of a proposal to a local council requesting the use of a vacant plot for a community garden.
writing.masterSentence: We propose to transform the disused lot on Mill Street into a community garden that would provide fresh produce, outdoor learning space and a shared meeting point for residents of all ages.
writing.stylistic: Collective 'we' voice, conditional 'would' for proposed outcomes, a tricolon of community backing, cost-benefit reframing ('a recurring liability into a maintained asset').

writing.title: A Public Apology after a Data Breach

meal.m: We let our customers down, and we are sorry: protecting your personal information is our responsibility, and on this occasion we failed to meet it.
meal.e: Last week, an outside party gained unlawful access to a database containing the names, email addresses and phone numbers of some of our customers; no payment details or passwords were stored in that system.
meal.a: We have closed the vulnerability, engaged independent security specialists to review our systems and informed the relevant data protection authority, but we know that these steps do not undo the anxiety this incident has caused.
meal.l: Every affected customer will be contacted directly with guidance on protecting themselves, and we will publish the findings of the independent review in full once it is complete.

writing.question: Write the key paragraph of a public statement in which a company issues an apology to customers after a data breach exposed their contact details.
writing.masterSentence: We let our customers down, and we are sorry: protecting your personal information is our responsibility, and on this occasion we failed to meet it.
writing.stylistic: An unhedged first-person apology placed first, short declarative clauses, plain vocabulary instead of legal euphemism, concrete commitments in the future simple.
